## Buying and investing

### Is a 10,000 to 20,000 SF building a sensible first industrial investment?

Buying and investing · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

I own some residential rentals and want to move into industrial. Is a small single-tenant building too risky as a first deal?

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

From the user side: small buildings are where companies like mine live. When we looked, there were very few choices under 20,000 SF with a decent yard.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

We see a lot of first-time industrial buyers at this size. The questions we ask are about the lease term versus the loan term, and your liquidity if the tenant leaves.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

It can be, if you underwrite the vacancy you will eventually have. A single-tenant building is either 100% leased or 0% leased, so the questions are how fast it would re-lease, what it would cost (downtime, improvements, commissions), and whether you could carry the debt and taxes meanwhile.

Small functional buildings in infill locations tend to have deep user demand, including owner-users who may buy it from you later. Read the single- versus multi-tenant discussion before you choose.

### Two buildings are listed at the same cap rate. Why would one be the better buy?

Buying and investing · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Same size, same county, same cap rate on the offering memorandum. How do I tell them apart?

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Look at what the tenants actually pay back. Two "NNN" leases can have very different recoveries once you read the CAM and roof language.

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

Ask how happy the tenant is. If we are about to outgrow a space, nothing in the rent roll shows it.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

The cap rate is one number from one year. Compare the rent each tenant pays against market rent, the remaining lease term, renewal options, expense recoveries, the roof and pavement age, the tax situation after a sale, and the building’s functionality for the next tenant.

A building with rent below market and a short lease can be the better buy at the same cap rate, because the income has room to grow, provided you can afford the rollover. Use the cap-rate calculator on your own adjusted NOI, not the marketing number.

### Should an investor ever buy a vacant industrial building?

Buying and investing · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Vacant buildings seem cheaper per square foot. What is the catch?

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Financing is the catch. Without leases we lend on a lower value with more equity, or we need a bridge loan with a higher rate.

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

You are competing with people like me. We can pay more for a vacant building because we plan to use it.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Sometimes. It is a value-add or lease-up strategy, and the price has to pay for the risk: months of carry (taxes, insurance, utilities, debt), improvements, commissions, and free rent. It works best for functional buildings in locations with steady demand and when you have the capital to wait.

Expect to compete with owner-users, who often finance with SBA 504 loans and can pay more than an investor can justify on rent alone. See owner-user vs. investor buyers .

### Should I buy industrial alone or with partners?

Buying and investing · 2 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

A few friends want to pool money. What should we work out before we buy?

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

We will want to know who signs the guaranty and who controls decisions. Unclear governance slows loans down.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Partnerships work when decision rights are clear before money moves. Agree in writing on who manages, how major decisions are made (sale, refinancing, capital calls, leasing), how cash is distributed, what happens if a partner cannot fund a capital call, and how someone exits.

Raising money from passive investors can involve securities law, so talk to an attorney before you advertise a deal or accept investor funds.

### How much cash should I keep in reserve after buying an industrial building?

Buying and investing · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Is there a rule of thumb for reserves on a small industrial property?

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Roofs, dock levelers, overhead doors, and parking lots are the usual big-ticket items. Most surprises are one of those.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Many loans require replacement reserves or tenant-improvement and leasing reserves anyway, especially when lease terms are short.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

There is no universal number. Build your reserve from the property condition assessment’s capital schedule, your lease rollover (downtime, improvements, commissions for the next expiration), and several months of taxes and debt service in case a tenant leaves.

In Illinois, budget specifically for property tax increases after the sale. See the tax underwriting section .

## Leasing and tenants

### As a tenant, what lease terms matter more than the rent?

Leasing and tenants · 3 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

We are renewing a 25,000 SF lease. Rent gets all the attention internally. What else should we push on?

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Restoration at move-out. Tenants forget about it until they get the bill for removing racking anchors and offices.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

From the landlord side, flexibility costs money. Expansion and termination rights are worth asking for, but expect to pay for them.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Total occupancy cost and flexibility. Check the expense pass-throughs (taxes, insurance, CAM, management fees, capital items), the repair and replacement responsibilities for the roof, HVAC, and docks, any renewal and expansion rights, assignment and sublease rights, restoration obligations, and the rights to use outdoor storage and trailer parking.

Compare offers as an all-in cost over the full term. The lease cost section shows how.

### My tenant is paying rent but has stopped operating in the building. Should I worry?

Leasing and tenants · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

The lights are off and the trucks are gone, but rent arrives on time.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Walk the building. Vacant buildings get roof leaks, frozen pipes, and break-ins, and nobody reports them.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Check your loan documents. Some have occupancy or insurance conditions that a dark building can trigger.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Yes, it is a signal to plan, even though it is not a default. Read the lease for any continuous-operation requirement, insurance conditions on vacancy, maintenance obligations, and sublease rights. Then talk with the tenant: an early termination or a sublease to a new user may be better for both of you than waiting out the term.

Start marketing conversations early, because industrial space can take months to re-lease.

### Our CAM reconciliation came in much higher than the estimate. What can we do?

Leasing and tenants · 2 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

The year-end true-up is several dollars per square foot higher than the budget.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Snow removal and property tax swings cause most big true-ups around Chicago. Ask for the detail by line item.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Ask for the reconciliation backup and compare it with the lease: which costs are recoverable, how your share is calculated, whether there are caps on controllable expenses, and whether capital replacements were passed through improperly. Many leases give tenants audit rights within a set time after receiving the statement.

In Chicagoland, property tax changes are often the biggest driver, so check whether the landlord appealed the assessment.

### Can we sign a one-year lease on industrial space?

Leasing and tenants · 3 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

We need space for a project that may last 12 to 18 months.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Short terms are hard for landlords because the commission and improvement costs barely pay back. Expect as-is space and higher rent.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Look for space that is already built out, or for a sublease with a short remaining term.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Sometimes, but expect trade-offs: as-is space, higher rent, fewer concessions, and possibly a larger deposit. Subleases with 12 to 24 months remaining, older multi-tenant buildings, and third-party logistics (3PL) warehousing are common short-term options.

If the need may extend, negotiate a renewal option now.

### Can we park trailers and store equipment outside a leased building?

Leasing and tenants · 2 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

Our operation needs space for about ten trailers and some equipment outside.

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We learned the hard way that the village cared even though the landlord did not.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Only if both the lease and the zoning allow it. Many municipalities restrict outdoor storage and trailer parking even in industrial districts, or they require screening, paving, and approval. Get the lease to grant the specific rights (area, number of trailers, hours) and confirm the zoning with the municipality.

See industrial outdoor storage for why yard rights are valuable.

## Building and operations

### Our roof is 20 years old. Repair it, restore it, or replace it?

Building and operations · 3 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We have a few leaks on a 40,000 SF building and want to plan for the next 10 years.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Get a core cut and moisture survey before deciding. Wet insulation usually rules out a coating.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

If you might sell in a few years, a buyer will price the roof anyway. A transferable warranty helps.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Have a roofing consultant do an infrared or moisture survey and take core samples. If the insulation is mostly dry, a restoration or coating system may extend the roof’s life at lower cost; if it is wet, replacement is usually the better long-term answer.

Either way, document the work and keep the warranties, because buyers and lenders will ask for them. See physical due diligence .

### Can we add dock doors to an existing industrial building?

Building and operations · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We have grade-level doors only and need to load semi-trailers.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Check the truck court first. A dock door is useless without room for the trailer to back in.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Often, yes. Common approaches are cutting the wall and excavating an exterior dock well, or building an interior pit with a leveler. Feasibility depends on the wall structure, the slab, drainage, utilities underground, truck-court depth, and permits.

Get an engineer and a contractor to scope it, and check stormwater rules for the dock well. Adding docks can widen a building’s tenant and buyer pool.

### How long does an electrical service upgrade take for a warehouse?

Building and operations · 3 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

We need more power for equipment and EV forklift charging.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

The utility timeline is usually the long pole, not the electrician.

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

Switchgear and transformer lead times have been long in recent years. Order early.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Plan for months, not weeks. The timeline depends on whether the utility needs to upgrade its transformer or line, equipment lead times for switchgear and transformers, engineering and permits, and lease negotiations over who pays and who owns the upgrade.

If power is critical, confirm the available capacity with the utility before you sign a lease or purchase agreement.

### Will our storage need a sprinkler upgrade in a building we are about to lease?

Building and operations · 2 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

We store plastic goods on racks about 24 feet high.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Prior tenants often stored something easier, so the existing system was fine for them. Ask for the sprinkler design data.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Possibly. Sprinkler adequacy depends on the commodity classification (plastics are typically more demanding), storage height and arrangement, building height, and water supply. Ask the landlord for the system’s design criteria and have a fire-protection engineer compare it with your storage plan before you sign.

Negotiate in the lease who pays if an upgrade or in-rack sprinklers are needed. The local fire department will have the final say.

### We are moving out of our building. What improvements help it lease or sell?

Building and operations · 3 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We plan to lease or sell our building after we relocate.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Buyers notice deferred maintenance immediately: roof, docks, lighting, pavement.

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

Clean, bright, and empty sells. LED lighting and working docks matter on a tour.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Focus on things that are cheap relative to how much they change a buyer’s perception: fix roof leaks, service dock equipment and doors, upgrade to LED lighting, repair pavement, clean and paint, remove abandoned equipment, and gather documents (permits, warranties, drawings, environmental reports).

Avoid custom improvements that only suit your operation. The selling guide covers preparation.

## Illinois taxes and incentives

### Our Cook County tax bill jumped after reassessment. Is an appeal worth it?

Illinois taxes and incentives · 3 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

Our assessed value rose much more than we expected.

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

Watch the township appeal window. In Cook it is short and the dates are published by the Assessor.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Appeals are routine for income property. Most owners appeal regularly.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Often it is worth reviewing. Compare the Assessor’s estimate of market value with what the property would actually sell for, given its income, vacancy, condition, and comparable sales. Appeals can be filed with the Assessor during the township window, then with the Board of Review, and potentially the Property Tax Appeal Board.

Many attorneys work on contingency. Details are in the appeals and deadlines section .

### Can an owner-user get the Class 6b incentive when buying a vacant building?

Illinois taxes and incentives · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We are looking at a building in Cook County that has been empty for a while.

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

Timing is critical. The application has to be filed on time, and the municipality’s support has to be in place.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

It is possible. Class 6b can apply to qualifying industrial property that is reoccupied after a period of vacancy, as well as new construction and substantial rehabilitation, if the municipality supports it and the application is timely. The rules on vacancy length, special circumstances, and filing deadlines are specific.

Check the Cook County Assessor’s current incentive requirements and talk to the municipality early, before closing. See What is Class 6b?

### How do I estimate taxes for a DuPage or Will County building I am buying?

Illinois taxes and incentives · 2 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

I am used to Cook County. What changes in the collar counties?

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

The township assessor is your first call. The supervisor of assessments and the Board of Review come next.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Outside Cook, property is generally assessed at one-third of market value by township assessors, with county equalization. Estimate the market value an assessor might apply after your purchase, apply the assessment level and the equalization factor, subtract exemptions, and multiply by the current tax rate for the property’s tax code.

Then confirm the result with the township assessor’s office. The Cook vs. collar county section explains the differences.

### Can a tenant appeal the property taxes on a building it leases?

Illinois taxes and incentives · 2 replies · Asked by Tenant operations (illustrative)

**Tenant operations** (Illustrative role · leases warehouse space):

We pay the taxes under our NNN lease. The landlord does not seem interested in appealing.

**Property manager** (Illustrative role · manages multi-tenant industrial):

Read the lease. Many leases say who controls appeals and how refunds are split.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Read the lease first: many NNN leases say who may file appeals and who receives refunds. Illinois appeal rules also determine who has standing. A tenant that pays the taxes often has a strong interest, and in practice many tenants ask the landlord to appeal or to allow an appeal at the tenant’s expense.

Talk to a property tax attorney about standing and deadlines before the appeal window closes.

### What do Illinois Enterprise Zones offer an industrial company?

Illinois taxes and incentives · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

Our broker mentioned that a site is inside an Enterprise Zone.

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

Benefits vary by zone. Each zone has its own administrator and local terms.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Illinois Enterprise Zones can offer incentives such as a state sales tax exemption on building materials, and local benefits such as property tax abatements, depending on the zone. Benefits, eligibility, and application steps vary by zone and change over time.

Contact the zone administrator and check the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity program pages. See the zones and TIFs section .

## Financing

### How does an SBA 504 loan work for buying our own warehouse?

Financing · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We are a growing distributor and want to buy instead of lease.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

The occupancy rules matter. For an existing building, the business generally needs to occupy at least 51%.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

An SBA 504 loan typically combines a bank first mortgage, a second loan from a Certified Development Company backed by the SBA, and a down payment from the business, often around 10% but higher in some cases. The 504 portion offers long-term fixed rates.

The business must meet SBA size and eligibility rules and generally occupy at least 51% of an existing building. See the SBA’s 504 program page and talk to a CDC early.

### Recourse or non-recourse debt on a small industrial building?

Financing · 2 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

My bank offers a better rate with a full personal guaranty.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Smaller loans from banks are usually recourse. Non-recourse is more common on larger loans and with life companies or CMBS lenders.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Compare the whole package, not just the rate. Recourse debt from a local bank can come with flexibility, relationship value, and lower costs, but it puts your personal assets at risk. Non-recourse loans limit that risk but typically carry “bad boy” carve-outs, stricter terms, and prepayment penalties such as yield maintenance or defeasance.

Some lenders offer partial recourse or burn-offs once a property stabilizes.

### How do prepayment penalties affect when I can sell?

Financing · 2 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

I want flexibility to sell in three to five years.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Step-down penalties, such as 3-2-1, are common on bank loans. Fixed-rate CMBS and life company loans tend to use yield maintenance or defeasance.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

A large prepayment penalty can effectively lock you into a hold or require a buyer to assume your loan. Match the loan’s prepayment terms to your realistic hold period, and ask whether the loan can be assumed by a buyer.

Model the penalty in your exit analysis at different interest rates, because yield maintenance gets more expensive when rates fall.

### Why do lenders discount income from leases that expire before the loan?

Financing · 2 replies · Asked by Commercial lender (illustrative)

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

A frequent borrower question we answer.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

This surprised me on my first deal. The building was full but the loan came in lower than expected.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Because the lender is underwriting the risk that the income stops. If the leases roll during the loan term, lenders may size the loan on lower rent or vacancy, require leasing reserves, add a cash sweep, or shorten the term.

Borrowers can improve proceeds by renewing leases early, showing tenant commitment, or providing reserves. See how lenders size loans .

### What happens to a loan if the Phase I finds a problem?

Financing · 2 replies · Asked by Commercial lender (illustrative)

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

Another common borrower question.

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

Ours found an old underground tank. It delayed closing by a few weeks while it was investigated.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

It depends on the finding. Lenders may require a Phase II, a remediation plan and cost estimate, escrow holdbacks, environmental insurance, an indemnity, or an Illinois EPA No Further Remediation letter before closing. Some lenders will decline.

Order the Phase I early so there is time to respond. See What is a Phase II?

## Selling and exit

### We own our building and are thinking about retiring. Sell, sale-leaseback, or lease it out?

Selling and exit · 3 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

The company may be sold separately from the real estate.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

A buyer of your company might want a lease from you. That lease can be what makes the real estate valuable.

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

Talk to your accountant about the tax basis and depreciation recapture before deciding.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Each path has trade-offs. A sale to an owner-user can pay well if the building is functional and you vacate. A sale-leaseback sets a lease and sells to an investor, which can work alongside a company sale. Keeping the building and leasing it gives income but keeps you as a landlord.

Coordinate the real estate plan with the business sale and your tax advisor. See sale-leasebacks and 1031 exchanges .

### My tenant’s lease expires in 18 months. Sell now or renew first?

Selling and exit · 3 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

I am worried a short lease hurts the price.

**Commercial lender** (Illustrative role · underwrites industrial loans):

A buyer’s lender will discount that income too, which affects what the buyer can pay.

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

Some buyers like me want the building when the lease ends.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

A renewal at market rent usually maximizes investor pricing, because it removes the biggest risk. But the short lease can attract owner-users who plan to occupy the building after expiration. Price both options: investor value with a renewal versus owner-user value with a planned vacancy.

If you negotiate a renewal, avoid concessions that cost more than the value they add.

### The buyer asked for a price cut after inspections. Is that normal?

Selling and exit · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

The roof and parking lot were raised as issues.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

As a buyer, I renegotiate when diligence finds something the marketing did not disclose. I do not when it was disclosed.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

It is common for buyers to ask for a credit when diligence finds real costs. The question is whether the issue was already known and priced. Ask for the reports, get your own repair estimate, and consider a credit, a repair before closing, or holding firm if the issue was disclosed.

Disclosing known problems up front and having documents ready reduces renegotiation. See the sale process .

### I am selling and doing a 1031 exchange. How do I avoid running out of time?

Selling and exit · 2 replies · Asked by Private investor (illustrative)

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

The 45-day identification window worries me.

**Tax consultant** (Illustrative role · works on Illinois assessments):

Set up your qualified intermediary before closing on the sale. You cannot touch the proceeds.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Start looking for replacement property before you close the sale, line up financing, and engage a qualified intermediary before closing. Identify replacement properties properly within 45 days and close within 180 days, under the identification rules your tax advisor recommends.

Some sellers negotiate a longer closing or a delayed closing to give more time. See What is a 1031 exchange?

### How do we sell our building without employees and customers finding out?

Selling and exit · 2 replies · Asked by Owner-user (illustrative)

**Owner-user** (Illustrative role · runs a company that owns its building):

We want to keep operating while we explore a sale.

**Private investor** (Illustrative role · owns leased industrial buildings):

Serious buyers expect to sign a confidentiality agreement and will tour after hours.

**Pavlo Rospopa** (Industrial investment sales · site author) (answer):

Use a targeted marketing process: qualified buyers only, confidentiality agreements before materials, no signs or public listings, tours after hours, and clear rules for contacting employees and tenants.

A broker can handle buyer screening. See confidentiality in the selling guide .

## About the participants

The roundtable roles (Owner-user, Private investor, Tenant operations, Commercial lender, Property manager, and Tax consultant) are composites I wrote to show how different sides of a transaction tend to think. They are not real people, and their posts are not quotes. The marked answers are mine, written as general education for the Chicagoland industrial market. For short answers, see the 100-question FAQ and the investor Q&A .

To ask your own question, or answer someone else’s, use the members' board .

> General education only. This is not legal, tax, environmental, engineering, lending, appraisal, or investment advice, and not a recommendation about any property. Members' board posts are the views of their authors. Verify facts and current rules with the responsible offices and qualified professionals before acting.

Industrial guide · Building function and specifications

# Industrial building types and specifications

This guide explains common industrial building types and the physical specifications buyers, tenants, lenders, and advisors review for 10,000 to 100,000 square foot assets in Chicagoland.

Published October 3, 2026 · Educational, not an engineering report or valuation.

## In brief

- Industrial labels are shorthand; the actual utility comes from loading, clear height, power, truck movement, fire protection, and zoning.
- A building can be excellent for one user and inefficient for another because operations, storage profile, labor, and equipment differ.
- Class A, B, and C descriptions are informal and should be tied to specific, verifiable features rather than marketing labels.
- Specifications should be confirmed from documents, site measurements, municipal records, and qualified professionals.
- For sellers, a clear spec sheet can reduce re-trading and help match the right buyer or tenant pool.

## Why type and spec matter for 10,000 to 100,000 SF buildings

In the 10,000 to 100,000 square foot range, many assets are bought by owner-users, private investors, and local or regional tenants. The same building may be evaluated as an operating facility, an income investment, or a future re-tenanting opportunity.

Owner-users often start with fit: doors, power, production flow, office area, parking, and expansion room. Tenants compare total occupancy cost, timing, lease obligations, and whether the site can support their operations without major disruption.

Investors review the current lease profile and then ask who else could use the building if the tenant leaves. That is why the industrial building evaluation checklist and the seller file described in the selling guide focus on function, records, and verifiable facts.

- Function: Does the building support the use without unusual workarounds?
- Flexibility: Could another user occupy it if the first plan changes?
- Risk: Are there physical, zoning, environmental, or utility constraints that affect timing or cost?

## Common industrial building types

Building-type names are useful starting points, but they are not substitutes for diligence. Verify the physical features, permitted use, and operating history before relying on a label.

**Industrial building types and what to verify**
- Type: Typical operations: Defining features: What to verify
- Bulk warehouse or distribution: Storage, fulfillment, wholesale distribution, and regional movement of goods.: Larger open warehouse areas, multiple dock-high positions, trailer movement, and racking potential.: Clear height , dock package, truck court, fire protection, trailer parking, and racking layout.
- Light industrial or small-bay: Service, trades, last-mile operations, small distribution, contractor storage, and local businesses.: Divisible suites, drive-in doors, modest office finish, and shared parking or yard areas.: Suite demising, utility metering, parking allocation, overhead doors, lease language, and permitted uses.
- Manufacturing: Production, assembly, fabrication, packaging, and repair. Heavy manufacturing usually has greater equipment, utility, ventilation, or process needs than light manufacturing.: Power, slab capacity, clear spans, ventilation, cranes, process piping, and separation between office and production areas.: Electrical service, floor loads, air permits, hazardous materials, equipment anchoring, floor drains, and zoning.
- Flex or office-warehouse: Showroom, research, light assembly, service, office support, and warehouse storage in one building.: Higher office percentage, storefront or customer entry, flexible warehouse area, and a mix of parking and loading.: Office buildout quality, HVAC zoning, parking, ceiling heights, loading, and whether office area can be reused economically.
- Cold storage or food-grade: Refrigerated, frozen, food handling, beverage, pharmaceutical, or temperature-sensitive distribution.: Insulated envelope, refrigeration systems, floor drains, washable surfaces, dock seals, and tight temperature controls.: Temperature zones, equipment age, sanitary design, backup power, permits, roof penetrations, and operating costs.
- Truck terminal or cross-dock: Freight transfer, route consolidation, parcel handling, and short-dwell movement.: Doors on opposing sides or high door count, shallow storage depth, large paved areas, and trailer circulation.: Cross-dock configuration, door spacing, pavement, ingress, egress, lighting, security, and hours of operation.
- Industrial outdoor storage or yard: Fleet parking, contractor yard, equipment storage, container storage, materials staging, and trailer parking.: Usable fenced land, stabilized surface, security, drainage, and limited building area.: Zoning, special-use approvals, surface condition, stormwater controls, screening, lighting, and neighbor constraints.
- Rail-served industrial: Bulk materials, manufacturing inputs, transload, plastics, metals, paper, lumber, and heavy commodities.: Rail spur or siding, loading doors, interior or exterior rail access, and agreements with a railroad or operator.: Active service, track condition, switch rights, clearance, commodity restrictions, easements, and maintenance obligations.
- Data or specialty industrial: Data, lab, clean manufacturing, life-safety, fleet electrification, or other specialized operations.: Unusual power, cooling, redundancy, security, floor loads, or regulatory requirements.: Utility commitments, cooling, code compliance, specialty permits, removal obligations, and whether improvements have reuse value.

## Specifications explained and why each matters

A useful spec sheet explains both the number and the practical effect. Where possible, separate measured facts from assumptions or broker shorthand.

- **Clear height**: Clear height is commonly measured from the finished floor to the lowest obstruction, not simply to the roof deck. It affects racking, equipment, lighting, and sprinkler design, and it should be checked against beams, joists, ducts, heaters, fans, and sprinkler piping.
- **Column spacing and speed bays**: Column spacing affects storage layout, forklift movement, production cells, and future demising. Speed bays near docks can provide staging depth for loading, but verify actual dimensions and obstructions.
- **Dock-high doors and door ratio**: Dock-high loading supports trailer-height movement and can be critical for distribution. Door-to-area ratios are a concept for comparing loading intensity, but the right ratio depends on the operation, trailer dwell, staffing, and truck scheduling.
- **Drive-in doors**: Drive-in doors allow vehicles, equipment, or vans to enter at grade. Verify clear opening, apron slope, door condition, security, and whether grade changes affect safe use.
- **Dock levelers, seals, shelters, and bumpers**: These components affect safety, weather protection, product handling, and dock efficiency. Condition, capacity, controls, and maintenance records should be reviewed during physical diligence.
- **Truck court depth and turning**: Truck circulation depends on court depth, trailer length, door angle, opposing parking, curbs, fences, and stored materials. A site plan should be tested against the intended truck type.
- **Trailer and car parking**: Trailer stalls, car stalls, fleet spaces, and visitor spaces serve different functions. Verify striping, easements, shared rights, zoning requirements, and whether outdoor storage is permitted.
- **Slab thickness, flatness, and load**: Slab performance matters for racking, forklifts, equipment, and high-bay storage. Concepts from ACI and ASTM standards may be relevant, but a structural engineer should verify thickness, joints, flatness, condition, and load capacity when material.
- **Power**: Record amps, voltage, phase, panels, switchgear, transformer location, spare capacity, and utility service. Three-phase power is often important for machinery, compressors, welders, refrigeration, and certain charging or process loads.
- **Lighting**: Lighting affects safety, productivity, and energy cost. Verify fixture type, controls, exterior lighting, emergency lighting, and measured light levels where operations require them.
- **Fire protection**: Wet-pipe systems, ESFR sprinklers , in-rack sprinklers, pumps, and alarms each support different storage designs. Commodity classification, storage height, rack layout, and the referenced NFPA 13 standard should be reviewed by a fire-protection engineer and the authority having jurisdiction.
- **Roof**: Roof type, age, remaining warranty, drainage, penetrations, insulation, and repair history affect capital planning. A roof consultant can separate routine maintenance from near-term replacement risk.
- **HVAC, ventilation, and warehouse heat**: Industrial HVAC is often uneven across office, production, and warehouse areas. Verify heaters, make-up air, exhaust, ventilation, cooling, controls, and code requirements for the proposed use.
- **Office finish percentage**: Office area can help administrative users and hurt users that need warehouse depth. Confirm rentable area, quality, HVAC service, restrooms, demising walls, and conversion cost.
- **Floor-to-floor height for mezzanines**: Mezzanines and two-level office areas depend on clearances, structure, stairs, egress, accessibility, and fire protection. Verify permits, load rating, and whether the mezzanine is included in reported square footage.
- **Site coverage and expansion land**: Low site coverage may allow yard, parking, or expansion, but zoning, setbacks, stormwater, utilities, easements, and wetlands can limit usable land. Do not assume vacant land is buildable.
- **Zoning and permitted use**: Zoning controls uses, outdoor storage, parking, signage, truck traffic, hours, and nonconforming rights. Confirm the actual intended use with the municipality rather than relying only on a zoning district name.

For safety and workplace requirements, start with applicable code officials and qualified professionals; federal OSHA materials may also be relevant to operations.

## Class A, B, and C as informal labels

Industrial class labels are market shorthand, not a single official standard. They can be useful only when tied to facts that can be inspected and documented.

**Informal ways people describe industrial building class**
- Label: Common description: Caution
- Class A: Newer or recently modernized building with stronger loading, height, systems, truck circulation, life-safety features, and institutional-quality records.: A small Class A building may still be wrong for a user if doors, power, or zoning do not fit.
- Class B: Functional building with some older features, moderate office finish, usable loading, and a condition profile that may require selective capital work.: Class B can be a broad category, so list the actual strengths and weaknesses.
- Class C: Older or more specialized building with lower clear height, limited loading, heavier deferred maintenance, or narrower reuse.: Class C does not mean unusable; it means the buyer pool may be more specific and diligence may be more important.

## How specs translate to buyer and tenant pools

Specifications shape demand because they determine who can operate efficiently. A property with strong doors, turning, power, and fire protection may appeal to a broader distribution or manufacturing audience than one with the same square footage but limited utility.

Functional obsolescence occurs when older features reduce usefulness compared with current operating needs. Examples include low clear height, shallow truck courts, insufficient power, limited parking, heavy office finish, difficult column spacing, or loading that does not match the building size.

Investors consider re-tenanting risk by asking how many users can realistically occupy the space, how long improvements might take, and what capital would be needed. For income-property context, see the investment diligence guide and the commercial leasing guide .

- Broader pool: flexible layout, adequate power, code-compliant improvements, documented systems, and common loading patterns.
- Narrower pool: very specialized equipment, unusual floor plan, unresolved environmental history, nonconforming yard, or limited truck access.
- Seller takeaway: disclose constraints clearly and support strengths with records rather than adjectives.

## Spec sheet checklist

A spec sheet should help a buyer, tenant, lender, or inspector confirm facts quickly. If a detail is unknown, mark it as to be verified rather than guessing.

**Items to include in an industrial property spec sheet**
- Item: Where to verify: Who verifies
- Building and land area: Survey, assessor records, appraisal, plans, leases, and measurement reports.: Surveyor, architect, appraiser, broker, or buyer representative.
- Clear height: Field measurement to lowest obstruction and building plans if available.: Broker, tenant, architect, engineer, or racking consultant.
- Column spacing: Plans, field measurement, and racking layout.: Architect, engineer, racking vendor, or tenant operations team.
- Dock and drive-in doors: Site tour, door schedule, dock equipment records, and photographs.: Broker, property manager, dock contractor, or inspector.
- Truck court and turning: ALTA survey, site plan, truck-turn exhibit, and field observation.: Civil engineer, surveyor, buyer, or logistics consultant.
- Parking and trailer storage: Striping plan, zoning file, lease rights, easements, and field count.: Broker, municipality, surveyor, or land-use attorney.
- Power service: Utility records, electrical one-line, panels, transformer, and electrician inspection.: Electrical contractor, engineer, utility, or tenant equipment vendor.
- Fire protection: Sprinkler drawings, inspection reports, hydraulic calculations, and alarm records.: Fire-protection contractor, engineer, insurer, and authority having jurisdiction.
- Roof: Warranty, roof plan, maintenance invoices, leak log, and roof report.: Roof consultant, contractor, inspector, or lender consultant.
- Slab: Plans, cores if appropriate, condition survey, and load review.: Structural engineer, concrete consultant, or buyer equipment vendor.
- HVAC and ventilation: Equipment schedules, service records, field inspection, and code review.: Mechanical contractor, engineer, or property condition assessor.
- Zoning and use: Municipal zoning map, zoning letter, permits, and certificates of occupancy.: Municipality, land-use attorney, buyer, or zoning consultant.
- Environmental history: Phase I ESA, permits, tank records, spill records, and owner interviews.: Environmental consultant and counsel.
- Title and survey matters: Title commitment , exception documents, ALTA survey , and recorded easements.: Title company, surveyor, and real estate attorney.

For regional research sources, the county hub links to assessment offices across Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties.

> This guide is general education, not engineering, environmental, legal, tax, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify measurements, code requirements, zoning, records, environmental matters, and transaction decisions with qualified professionals before acting.

Operations & property suitability

# Evaluating Chicago industrial real estate

Industrial space has to work for the operation inside it. Before comparing a warehouse for lease or an industrial building for sale, translate storage, production, loading, and staffing needs into a written building checklist.

Published October 2, 2026 · No current inventory or market statistics are represented.

## In brief

- Before touring, translate the operation (storage, production, loading, staffing) into a written building checklist.
- Verify clear height, loading, truck court, slab, power, and fire protection with measurements and professional review, not listing figures.
- Test real routes, truck restrictions, and site access; highway or rail proximity does not prove usable freight access.
- Review flood exposure and environmental history, and commission diligence appropriate to the transaction.

_Warehouse interior with selective pallet racking: clear height, column spacing, lighting, and floor condition all affect how a building works._

## Match the actual use, not just the label

- **Warehouse and distribution**: Storage layout, throughput, racking, fire protection, dock capacity, and trailer circulation matter alongside building size.
- **Logistics and last-mile operations**: Test routes to actual customers or destinations, vehicle access, dispatch patterns, parking, and permitted operating hours. Straight-line distance does not establish delivery time.
- **Manufacturing**: Equipment loads, process utilities, ventilation, wastewater, vibration, noise, and any required permits should be reviewed by qualified specialists.
- **Flex space**: Office and industrial areas can have different physical and code requirements. Confirm the permitted activity, buildout scope, and whether the mix can support the intended business.

Write down pallet or equipment dimensions, inventory type, peak daily vehicle movements, shifts, and growth assumptions. Special storage or processes may introduce requirements that a generic listing does not address.

## A building-fit checklist

**Items to verify before leasing or purchasing**
- Feature: What to verify
- Clear height and columns: Measure usable clearance below obstructions, not just roof height. Review column spacing against the equipment and storage layout.
- Loading: Identify dock-high and drive-in doors, their dimensions and condition, equipment, staging area, and shared-use restrictions.
- Truck court and yard: Test turning and backing with the actual vehicle type. Confirm trailer parking, outdoor storage permissions, access rights, and snow-storage arrangements.
- Floor and structure: Have qualified professionals assess slab condition, flatness, load capacity, and any proposed equipment or rack anchoring.
- Power and utilities: Verify voltage, phase, service capacity, and available capacity with equipment needs and utility providers. An upgrade’s cost and schedule require confirmation.
- Fire protection: Confirm that the installed system and approved storage arrangement suit the commodity, packaging, rack design, and proposed storage height.
- Roof and building systems: Review condition, maintenance records, remaining service life, and responsibility for repairs or replacement.
- People and access: Check employee and visitor parking, accessible facilities, restrooms, office needs, ventilation, and safe separation of pedestrian and vehicle activity.

Do not infer suitability from an advertised clear height, number of docks, or power rating. Request supporting information and confirm it through measurements and professional review.

## Research the location as an operating network

For Chicago-area industrial property, evaluate the actual routes between the building, suppliers, customers, freight facilities, and employees. Check local truck restrictions, bridge or clearance constraints, highway access, and traffic at relevant operating times. Proximity to an airport, rail terminal, or expressway does not prove practical freight access.

Compare local research paths in the Chicagoland industrial real estate hub : Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry, and Will counties in Illinois, USA. Each county section connects operational questions with official jurisdiction, planning, zoning, or parcel sources. This defined scope does not include Indiana or Wisconsin.

Confirm the municipality and county before researching zoning. Outdoor storage, truck parking, production, and extended hours need property-specific review. Use the commercial property research guide to organize zoning, tax, and building-record checks.

Review flood and drainage exposure and historical property uses. Commission environmental diligence appropriate to the transaction; a clean-looking warehouse does not establish that the land is free from contamination.

## Bring these questions to the tour

- What is verified, what is estimated, and what still needs an inspection?
- Can the exact operation be permitted here, including storage and vehicle activity?
- Which improvements are required before occupancy, who pays, and what is the approval schedule?
- Are loading, yard, parking, or utilities shared with other occupants?
- Who maintains and replaces the roof, structure, docks, pavement, and fire-protection system?
- What limits expansion, assignment, subleasing, or later resale?

For a lease, use the occupancy-cost and lease checklist . For a purchase, review acquisition diligence and financing risk . A low quoted rent or purchase price may not offset a costly operational mismatch.

## Official sources for follow-up

- Chicago zoning map and Department of Buildings : city zoning and building research; suburban authorities are separate.
- Chicago Metropolitan Agency for Planning : regional transportation and planning context.
- FEMA Flood Map Service Center : mapped flood hazards.
- EPA: All Appropriate Inquiries : environmental due-diligence background for acquisitions, not a property clearance.

> This is a general evaluation framework, not engineering, fire-code, environmental, or legal advice. Obtain property-specific advice before committing to equipment, construction, a lease, or a purchase.

Industrial guide · Physical and environmental diligence

# Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental

This guide organizes the physical, environmental, title, survey, zoning, lease, and utility questions that commonly affect industrial property acquisitions across the nine Illinois counties covered by these guides.

Published October 3, 2026 · Educational, not legal, environmental, engineering, or investment advice.

## In brief

- Industrial diligence is different because prior uses, heavy systems, loading, utilities, and environmental history can drive value and closing risk.
- The purchase agreement should control deadlines, access, seller deliverables, and remedies for findings.
- Environmental review often starts with a Phase I ESA and may expand to sampling, vapor, tanks, asbestos, lead, or regulatory closure issues.
- Physical diligence should convert roof, slab, dock, utility, fire-protection, pavement, and drainage findings into a capital plan.
- Findings usually become a decision about price, credits, escrows, repairs, insurance, indemnities, or whether to proceed.

## Why industrial diligence is different

Industrial property diligence is not limited to rent, taxes, and a walk-through. Past and current operations may involve chemicals, fuels, tanks, floor drains, heavy equipment, vehicle repair, food handling, manufacturing residues, or unusual utility loads.

Physical systems also carry deal risk. A roof, slab, dock package, sprinkler system, transformer, truck court, or drainage problem can change occupancy timing and capital needs.

For a broader acquisition framework, see the investment diligence guide . For building-fit questions, use the industrial evaluation checklist and the building types and specifications guide .

## Organizing the diligence period

The purchase and sale agreement should state when the diligence period starts, what the seller must deliver, what access is allowed, and what happens if the buyer objects. Calendar every notice date before ordering reports.

Access needs should be specific. Environmental consultants, roofers, surveyors, engineers, lenders, insurers, contractors, appraisers, and utility representatives may need different site visits, tenant coordination, and sampling permissions.

Sellers can reduce friction by pre-assembling the documents listed in the selling guide . A clean file does not replace diligence, but it helps buyers and lenders ask better questions.

- Use a diligence tracker with document status, responsible party, deadline, and open issue.
- Require insurance, safety rules, and escort procedures for invasive or operationally sensitive inspections.
- Coordinate tenant notices and quiet-hours if the property is occupied.
- Reserve enough time for follow-up testing when the initial report identifies a concern.

## Environmental diligence

Environmental work is usually scoped by the property history, intended use, lender requirements, and the buyer's risk tolerance. The consultant and legal counsel should explain the standard, reliance language, and any data gaps.

### Phase I ESA and AAI

A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment is commonly prepared under ASTM E1527-21 and federal All Appropriate Inquiries concepts. The U.S. EPA All Appropriate Inquiries page explains the federal framework and links to current rules.

The scope commonly includes records review, historical sources, site reconnaissance, interviews, and a report identifying recognized environmental conditions. The user also has responsibilities, such as providing specialized knowledge, commonly known information, and information about purchase price or environmental liens when applicable.

AAI has timing rules: the inquiry must be conducted or updated within one year before acquisition, and certain components must be conducted or updated within 180 days. Confirm current requirements and reliance language with the environmental consultant and counsel.

### RECs, HRECs, and CRECs

A recognized environmental condition, or REC, points to a likely presence or release of hazardous substances or petroleum products. A historical recognized environmental condition, or HREC, generally indicates a past release that has been addressed to the applicable standard.

A controlled recognized environmental condition, or CREC, generally means a past release remains subject to controls, restrictions, or ongoing obligations. The words matter because they can affect lender review, buyer obligations, and future use.

### Phase II sampling and vapor intrusion

A Phase II investigation may include soil, groundwater, soil-gas, indoor air, or other sampling. The purpose is to test specific concerns, not to prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property.

Vapor intrusion review can be important where volatile chemicals or petroleum releases may migrate into buildings. Sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design should be handled by qualified environmental professionals.

### Asbestos, lead, PCBs, USTs, and other regulated materials

Older industrial buildings may require separate review for asbestos-containing materials, lead-based paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground storage tanks, aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. These are often outside a basic Phase I scope unless specifically added.

Ask whether the consultant recommends targeted surveys before demolition, renovation, financing, or occupancy. Removal and disposal rules can affect timing and cost.

### Illinois EPA SRP and NFR letters

The Illinois EPA Site Remediation Program is a voluntary cleanup program that can lead to a No Further Remediation letter for addressed conditions. An NFR letter is not the same as saying every environmental risk is gone.

Review the recorded terms, institutional controls, engineered barriers, exposure routes, and future-use limits. Counsel and the consultant should confirm whether the proposed use remains consistent with the closure.

### Landowner liability protections

Federal landowner liability protections are concept-based and fact-specific. They may depend on proper AAI, continuing obligations, no affiliation issues, and conduct after acquisition.

Do not treat a report alone as a guarantee. Review the facts with environmental counsel before relying on any protection.

## Physical diligence

Physical diligence should identify current condition, code or safety concerns, near-term repairs, long-term capital needs, and operational constraints. A property condition assessment may reference ASTM E2018 concepts through ASTM , but the scope should match the asset and the deal.

### Roof, structure, and slab

Review roof age, membrane type, warranty, leaks, drainage, penetrations, insulation, repairs, and replacement timing. For structure and slab, inspect settlement, cracking, joints, floor flatness, load capacity, mezzanines, roof framing, and signs of impact or water intrusion.

### Docks, doors, and equipment

Dock levelers, bumpers, seals, shelters, overhead doors, drive-in doors, controls, and restraints affect safety and operations. Field-test condition where practical and compare the loading package to the intended use.

### Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing review should cover remaining useful life, capacity, code concerns, maintenance records, and tenant-specific modifications. Electrical capacity should be confirmed against panels, service, transformer, utility data, and equipment requirements.

For fire protection, ask for sprinkler inspection reports, alarm records, deficiencies, hydraulic calculations, fire-pump tests if applicable, and any storage or commodity assumptions. Verify sprinkler design with a fire-protection engineer, insurer, and authority having jurisdiction.

### Pavement, drainage, and flood

Pavement matters for trailers, forklifts, snow removal, drainage, and yard use. Inspect asphalt, concrete, catch basins, detention, ponding, striping, curbs, and truck-wear areas.

Flood and drainage review should include local records and the FEMA Flood Map Service Center . FEMA mapping does not replace a civil engineer's review of site drainage or stormwater obligations.

### Accessibility, elevators, and cranes

Accessibility review should consider parking, routes, entrances, restrooms, office areas, signage, and any alterations. Elevators, hoists, cranes, bridge cranes, and jib cranes require records, load ratings, inspections, service contracts, and ownership clarification.

### Deferred maintenance and capital plan

Convert inspection notes into a capital plan with timing, cost ranges, responsible party, and business impact. Separate immediate life-safety items from monitor-and-maintain items and future improvements.

## Title, survey, and land

Title and survey review connects legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey helps show boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments.

Review access rights, shared drive agreements, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage rights, recorded covenants, and any reciprocal easement agreements. A truck entrance that crosses another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use.

For rail-served property, confirm rail agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and whether the railroad or a third party controls access. Rail value can disappear if the legal and physical service rights do not match the marketing description.

## Zoning and permits

Zoning diligence should confirm the current district, permitted uses, special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours of operation. A zoning verification letter can help document how the municipality views the property.

Permits and certificates of occupancy show whether past work and uses were approved. Check for open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements that may need closeout.

For local research starting points, use the nine-county hub and municipal records. For Chicago-specific research, see the Chicago commercial real estate guide .

## Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial

Lease diligence should test whether the income, obligations, and operational rights shown in the rent roll are supported by signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and notice relevant to occupancy.

- Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims.
- SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change.
- CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances.
- Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements.
- Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports.
- Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles.

The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

## Utilities and infrastructure

Industrial users often need utility confirmation before they can commit. Electricity, gas, water, sanitary sewer, storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom should be reviewed against the user's equipment and occupancy schedule.

For much of the region, electrical capacity questions may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the tenant's equipment vendor. Confirm service voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements.

Gas, water, and sewer review should include meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. Fiber and telecom are separate from an address being generally serviceable.

## Turning findings into price, credits, escrows, or repairs

Diligence findings are useful only when they lead to a clear decision. The buyer can accept the risk, renegotiate price, request a credit, create an escrow, require seller repairs, modify representations, obtain insurance, or terminate if the contract allows.

Sellers should distinguish between documented defects, buyer preferences, and speculative future upgrades. Buyers should distinguish between ordinary maintenance and issues that change value, financing, insurability, or lawful use.

Material findings should be tied to evidence: report page, photo, contractor proposal, municipal response, title exception, lease clause, or consultant memo. That keeps negotiations focused on facts.

## Diligence checklist

This checklist is a starting point. The actual scope should match the property type, contract, lender, tenant, intended use, and risk tolerance.

**Industrial property diligence checklist**
- Item: Purpose: Typical provider
- Phase I ESA / AAI: Review historical and current environmental risk and support liability-protection analysis.: Environmental consultant and environmental counsel.
- Phase II or targeted sampling: Test specific concerns from records, site conditions, or Phase I findings.: Environmental consultant and laboratory.
- Asbestos, lead, PCB, tank, and regulated-material surveys: Identify special handling, renovation, demolition, or closure issues.: Specialty environmental consultant.
- Property condition assessment: Evaluate building systems, immediate repairs, and capital needs.: Engineer, architect, or PCA consultant.
- Roof report: Assess roof condition, leaks, warranty, drainage, and replacement timing.: Roof consultant or qualified contractor.
- Structural and slab review: Confirm load, cracking, settlement, mezzanines, cranes, and equipment impacts.: Structural engineer.
- MEP review: Confirm capacity, useful life, code concerns, and maintenance requirements.: Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing contractors or engineers.
- Fire-protection review: Confirm inspections, deficiencies, design assumptions, and storage compatibility.: Fire-protection contractor, engineer, insurer, and AHJ.
- Pavement and drainage review: Evaluate truck areas, ponding, stormwater, catch basins, and yard surface.: Civil engineer or pavement consultant.
- Title commitment and exception documents: Identify liens, requirements, easements, covenants, and recorded restrictions.: Title company and real estate attorney.
- Survey: Show boundaries, improvements, access, encroachments, easements, and parking or yard layout.: Licensed surveyor.
- Zoning verification: Confirm permitted use, nonconforming rights, parking, outdoor storage, and open violations.: Municipality, zoning consultant, and land-use attorney.
- Lease and tenant file review: Confirm rent, term, options, obligations, recoveries, defaults, and use rights.: Real estate attorney, broker, property manager, and buyer.
- Utility confirmation: Verify electric, gas, water, sewer, fire flow, and communication service for the intended use.: Utilities, engineers, contractors, and tenant equipment vendors.
- Capital plan and negotiation summary: Translate findings into price, credit, escrow, repair, insurance, or closing decisions.: Buyer, broker, counsel, lender, consultants, and seller.

For terminology, the Phase I ESA / AAI , ALTA survey , and title commitment glossary entries provide plain-English definitions.

> This guide is general education, not engineering, environmental, legal, tax, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Verify environmental conditions, building systems, title, survey, zoning, leases, utilities, and transaction decisions with qualified professionals before acting.

Market orientation · Illinois logistics corridors

# Chicagoland industrial submarkets and logistics corridors

A geography-first orientation to industrial clusters, freight infrastructure, and location diligence across the Illinois counties around Chicago.

Published October 3, 2026 · No rent, vacancy, pricing, or ranking claims.

## In brief
- Submarket names are brokerage conventions, not legal boundaries.
- Always verify the parcel’s municipality, county, zoning, truck routes, utilities, and tax district.
- Corridors often follow interstate, tollway, airport, rail, and intermodal access.
- Aurora, Elgin, Joliet, and other municipalities can cross county lines, so county assumptions must be checked.
- This guide describes geography and infrastructure only; it does not rank submarkets or state market statistics.

## How to use submarket labels

Industrial submarket names are shorthand. They help brokers, lenders, owners, and tenants talk about geography, but they are not zoning districts, tax districts, or municipal boundaries. A data provider may draw “O’Hare,” “I-55,” or “Joliet” differently from a broker or municipality.

Before underwriting a 10,000 to 100,000 square foot building, verify the parcel’s county and municipality using the nine-county industrial research hub . Then match the address to zoning, permitted use, truck routes, taxes, and utilities. A building can be marketed under one corridor name while legally sitting in a different taxing body or approval jurisdiction.

### Practical use

Use labels for search and tours; use legal records for closing, financing, zoning, environmental review, and municipal approvals.

## Corridors and clusters described by geography

### O?Hare corridor

Elk Grove Village, Bensenville, Wood Dale, Franklin Park, Schiller Park, and Des Plaines are tied to I-90, I-294, I-190, and O?Hare air cargo. Verify county, municipality, truck circulation, and airport-adjacent restrictions.

### North Cook and Lake County

Northbrook, Wheeling, Buffalo Grove, Lincolnshire, Libertyville, Gurnee, and Waukegan relate to I-94, US-41, and local arterials. Lake County means Illinois, not Indiana.

### Northwest and I-90

Schaumburg, Hoffman Estates, Elgin, Huntley, and the Belvidere direction follow I-90. Boone County is outside scope, and Elgin crosses county lines.

### Central DuPage, I-355 and I-88

Addison, Carol Stream, West Chicago, Glendale Heights, Lombard, Naperville, and Aurora relate to I-355, I-88, North Avenue, Roosevelt Road, and DuPage Airport. Aurora and Naperville cross county lines.

### West Cook, I-290 and inner I-55

Bedford Park, McCook, Hodgkins, Cicero, Bellwood, Melrose Park, and Northlake form an infill logistics belt near BNSF Cicero, CSX Bedford Park, and Union Pacific Global 2.

### I-55 corridor

Bolingbrook, Romeoville, Woodridge, Lemont, and Plainfield are commonly grouped along I-55, I-355, and nearby arterials across Will, DuPage, and Cook County.

### I-80 and Joliet area

Joliet, Elwood, Channahon, Minooka, Shorewood, University Park, and Monee are oriented to I-80 and I-55. BNSF Logistics Park Chicago and Union Pacific Global 4 are key reference points.

### South Cook, I-57 and I-294

Alsip, Bridgeview, Chicago Heights, Harvey, Markham, Matteson, and South Holland sit near I-57, I-294, I-80, and Calumet-area rail infrastructure, including Norfolk Southern, CN, and other rail references.

### City of Chicago industrial corridors

The City of Chicago uses official industrial corridor planning and Planned Manufacturing District tools. See the Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative .

### Kane, Kendall, DeKalb, McHenry, and Grundy outer markets

Aurora, Batavia, Geneva, St. Charles, Yorkville, Oswego, Plano, DeKalb, Sycamore, Woodstock, Crystal Lake, and Morris are smaller clusters tied to I-88, the I-39 direction, and I-80 west.

## Freight infrastructure overview

Freight infrastructure should be treated as a location attribute, not a guarantee. A building can be near a terminal or airport and still have poor truck access, wrong zoning, inadequate loading, or limited yard depth.

### Intermodal terminals and rail references

**Selected Chicago-area freight facilities to verify with official railroad sources**
- Facility: Railroad: Municipality or area: County: Official source
- Cicero Intermodal: BNSF: Cicero: Cook: BNSF facility listings
- Logistics Park Chicago: BNSF: Elwood: Will: BNSF facility listing
- Global 2: Union Pacific: Northlake: Cook: Union Pacific Global 2
- Global 4: Union Pacific: Joliet: Will: Union Pacific Global 4
- Bedford Park Intermodal: CSX: Bedford Park: Cook: CSX intermodal
- Landers: Norfolk Southern: Chicago: Cook: Norfolk Southern
- Chicago/Harvey terminal: CN: Harvey area: Cook: CN intermodal terminals

### Airports, interstates and tollways

**Air and highway references for industrial location review**
- Category: Examples: Source to check
- Air cargo: O’Hare cargo; Midway for airport adjacency; Chicago Rockford as a regional cargo point outside the nine-county scope.: FlyChicago cargo
- Tollways: I-90, I-294, I-355, I-88, and other Illinois Tollway facilities.: Illinois Tollway
- State and interstate routes: I-55, I-57, I-80, I-39 direction, US-41, and state-maintained arterials.: Illinois Department of Transportation

## How location factors enter underwriting

For 10,000 to 100,000 square foot industrial buildings, location underwriting is usually specific and practical. A small user or private investor cares about the actual drive, dock, labor, and approval path more than a broad corridor label.

### Factors to test
- Labor access: shift timing, transit availability, parking, and commute patterns.
- Truck routes: municipal restrictions, bridge clearances, road weight limits, turning movements, and neighborhood constraints.
- Last-mile versus regional distribution: customer proximity, expressway access, driver hours, and delivery window reliability.
- Tollway costs: repeated toll exposure can affect operating cost even when the route is efficient.
- Building function: clear height, loading, truck court, yard, power, sprinklers, office ratio, and expansion area. See the industrial building guide .

Nearby infrastructure does not replace property-level diligence. A building can sit near I-55 and still have a difficult left turn, shallow dock apron, or ordinance that limits trailer storage.

## Verification steps before relying on a submarket

Use this sequence before marketing a building, signing an LOI, or budgeting improvements.

### Checklist
- Confirm the address, PIN, county, municipality, township, school district, and fire district in the county hub .
- Verify zoning, legal nonconforming status, outdoor storage, parking, truck routes, and hours of operation with the municipality.
- Review utilities: electric service, gas, water, sanitary, stormwater, fire protection, and available capacity.
- Check access: curb cuts, easements, shared drives, rail rights, signal timing, bridge limits, and municipal truck-route maps.
- Compare the building to the user need: loading, clear height, power, office finish, yard, floor condition, and expansion land.
- Review taxes, incentives, TIFs, enterprise zones, and transfer taxes with the Illinois industrial property tax guide .

## Sources

These links are starting points for official verification. Use parcel, terminal, airport, tollway, and municipal sources together.

### Official and operator sources
- City of Chicago Industrial Corridor Modernization Initiative
- Chicago Department of Aviation cargo information
- BNSF facility listings
- Union Pacific Global 2 and Union Pacific Global 4
- CSX intermodal , Norfolk Southern , and CN intermodal terminals
- Illinois Tollway and Illinois Department of Transportation

For sale, lease, or investment context, cross-check selling industrial property , commercial leasing , commercial investment , and the glossary .

> This guide is general education, not legal, zoning, engineering, environmental, logistics, appraisal, brokerage, or investment advice. Submarket labels and freight references change by source and project. Verify jurisdiction, zoning, truck routes, utilities, tax records, incentives, and infrastructure access with official offices and qualified professionals before acting.
